CA.summary: California's grid was built on big hydro and natural gas, then shaken apart by the 2000-01 deregulation crisis that brought rolling blackouts. The state rebuilt around clean energy: a million solar roofs, a legal promise of 100% clean power by 2045, and giant batteries that store sunshine for the evening. Today gas still leads, but solar is a strong No. 2 and climbing.

events.title: Diablo Canyon nuclear plant opens
events.text: PG&E's twin reactors on the coast near San Luis Obispo start running. They make about 2,200 megawatts — enough clean power for roughly 3 million homes.

events.title: California deregulates its power market
events.text: Lawmakers pass AB 1890, letting power be bought and sold on open markets. The change was supposed to lower bills — but it set the stage for a crisis.

events.title: Rolling blackouts and the Enron crisis
events.text: Power prices exploded and the lights went out for millions. Traders at Enron gamed the new market, and the state lost tens of billions of dollars.

events.title: Million Solar Roofs law
events.text: Governor Schwarzenegger signs SB 1, offering big rebates to put solar panels on homes. California hit one million solar roofs in 2019.

events.title: San Onofre nuclear plant shuts down
events.text: Faulty new steam generators forced the plant to close for good. The state lost about 2,200 megawatts of carbon-free power overnight.

events.title: SB 100 sets 100% clean power goal
events.text: Governor Jerry Brown signs a law requiring all retail electricity to come from clean sources by 2045. It made California's clean energy push the law of the land.

events.title: Diablo Canyon gets a reprieve
events.text: Worried about blackouts, lawmakers pass SB 846 to keep the state's last nuclear plant open up to five more years. It still supplies about 9% of California's power.

signature_plant.name: Diablo Canyon Power Plant
signature_plant.fact: California's last nuclear plant. Its two reactors make about 9% of the state's electricity with zero carbon emissions.

TX.summary: Texas runs its own grid, ERCOT, mostly cut off from the rest of the country. In 1999 it threw open its power market to competition, and cheap land plus a $7 billion transmission build-out turned the state into America's wind capital. The deadly 2021 winter blackouts showed the risks of going it alone. Since then, Texas has added more solar and batteries than any other state.

events.title: South Texas Project nuclear opens
events.text: The first of two giant reactors near Bay City starts running. Together they make about 2,560 megawatts of carbon-free power for the Gulf Coast.

events.title: Texas deregulates its power market
events.text: Governor George W. Bush signs SB 7, letting Texans pick their electricity company. It also locked in ERCOT as the state's own separate grid.

events.title: Texas becomes No. 1 in wind
events.text: Texas zooms past California to lead the country in wind power. Big open ranches in West Texas and the Panhandle were perfect for turbines.

events.title: CREZ transmission lines finished
events.text: A $7 billion network of new power lines connects windy West Texas to the big cities. It unlocked over 18,000 megawatts of wind — more than enough for 4 million homes.

events.title: Winter Storm Uri blackouts
events.text: A brutal February freeze knocked out power for over 4.5 million homes. Hundreds of Texans died, mostly because natural gas equipment froze.

events.title: Solar and batteries surge
events.text: Texas added more new solar and battery storage than any other state. Big batteries soak up daytime sun and push it back to the grid after dark.

events.title: Solar passes coal
events.text: For the first time over a full year, solar made more electricity for the Texas grid than coal did. Solar reached about 14% of the grid; coal kept slipping.

signature_plant.name: Comanche Peak Nuclear Power Plant
signature_plant.fact: Its two reactors near Glen Rose started up in 1990 and 1993 and quietly power roughly 2 million Texas homes, day and night.

WA.summary: Washington's grid was built on big New Deal dams on the Columbia River, with Grand Coulee at its heart. Cheap hydropower drew aluminum smelters and, decades later, data centers. A 1980s plan to build five nuclear plants ended in the biggest municipal bond default in U.S. history — nicknamed 'Whoops.' Today hydro still makes most of the state's power, and a 2019 law requires 100% clean electricity by 2045.

events.title: Bonneville Power Administration created
events.text: President Roosevelt signs a law creating BPA to sell electricity from the new federal dams. It brought cheap power to farms and small towns.

events.title: Grand Coulee Dam finished
events.text: The huge concrete dam on the Columbia River starts making power. During World War II it ran factories building planes, ships, and atomic bomb material.

events.title: Grand Coulee becomes biggest US power plant
events.text: A third powerhouse pushes its capacity to 6,809 megawatts. It is still the largest power plant in the country — of any kind.

events.title: The 'Whoops' nuclear default
events.text: Washington Public Power Supply System defaulted on $2.25 billion in bonds after canceling two half-built nuclear plants. It was the biggest public bond bust in U.S. history.

events.title: Columbia Generating Station opens
events.text: The lone survivor of that nuclear plan starts running near Richland. At about 1,207 megawatts, it is still the state's only nuclear plant.

events.title: Clean Energy Transformation Act
events.text: Governor Inslee signs CETA, requiring utilities to drop coal by 2025 and be 100% clean by 2045. Hydro gave Washington a big head start.

events.title: Coal power ends in Washington
events.text: Under CETA's deadline, utilities stop selling Washington customers electricity made from coal. The grid leans even harder on hydro, wind, and nuclear.

signature_plant.name: Grand Coulee Dam
signature_plant.fact: Still the largest power plant in the United States. During World War II its power helped build planes, ships, and atomic bomb material.

WV.summary: For more than a century, West Virginia coal has fueled the country — and the state itself. Even today, coal makes about 86% of its electricity, the highest share of any state. Cheap natural gas has closed many coal plants since 2005, but giants like John Amos keep running, and state leaders are betting on coal and gas to power a new wave of data centers.

events.title: Coal country powers America
events.text: After the famous Mine Wars between miners and operators, West Virginia coal kept powering America's factories and homes. Coal became part of the state's identity.

events.title: John Amos Plant opens
events.text: The huge coal plant on the Kanawha River starts running. At about 2,933 megawatts, it is the biggest power plant in the state — enough for over 2 million homes.

events.title: Mountaineer tests carbon capture
events.text: Engineers at the Mountaineer coal plant tested catching carbon dioxide before it left the smokestack. The pilot worked, but shut down after a few years because no law made it pay.

events.title: Old coal plants start retiring
events.text: The 65-year-old Philip Sporn plant shut down — one of about ten coal plants closed in West Virginia since 2005 as cheap natural gas took over.

events.title: State doubles down on coal
events.text: Regulators approved upgrades to keep the Amos, Mountaineer, and Mitchell coal plants running until 2040. West Virginia bet on coal staying central.

events.title: Data centers push up bills
events.text: The regional grid's yearly payment to power plants jumped from $2.2 billion to $14.7 billion, raising West Virginia bills. Data centers next door in Virginia are the main reason.

events.title: The '50 by 50' plan
events.text: Governor Morrisey unveils a plan to triple the state's power capacity to 50 gigawatts by 2050, leaning on coal and natural gas, to attract data centers.

signature_plant.name: John E. Amos Power Plant
signature_plant.fact: One of the largest coal plants east of the Mississippi. Its three cooling towers are a landmark you can see for miles along Interstate 64.

GA.summary: Georgia's grid grew up around Georgia Power, with Plant Scherer near Macon long ranked the biggest coal plant in America. Then the state did something nobody had done in decades: it built two brand-new nuclear reactors at Plant Vogtle, finished in 2023 and 2024 for about $35 billion. Rural Georgia has also become a big solar producer — and now a data-center boom is driving plans for a huge new wave of power.

events.title: Plant Scherer opens
events.text: The huge coal plant near Juliette starts running. With 3,520 megawatts across four units, it became the largest coal-fired power plant in the United States.

events.title: Plant Vogtle Units 1 and 2 open
events.text: Georgia Power's first two reactors near Waynesboro start producing carbon-free power. They quickly became a big chunk of the state's electricity.

events.title: Georgia approves new Vogtle reactors
events.text: Regulators sign off on two new reactors at Vogtle — the first new U.S. nuclear construction in about 30 years. Customers started paying for them on their bills before they were built.

events.title: Scherer's biggest unit shuts down
events.text: Two Florida utilities retired Unit 4 of Plant Scherer, cutting 848 megawatts of coal. Cheap natural gas made the old plant too expensive to run.

events.title: Vogtle Unit 3 starts up
events.text: The first newly built U.S. reactor in seven years comes online in Georgia. It makes about 1,100 megawatts — enough for half a million homes.

events.title: Vogtle Unit 4 finishes the project
events.text: The second new reactor begins commercial operation. The full Vogtle expansion cost about $35 billion — more than double the original budget.

events.title: Massive expansion for data centers
events.text: Regulators approved Georgia Power's plan to add 10,000 megawatts of new capacity, mostly natural gas, to feed data-center growth. About 80% of the new power would serve data centers.

signature_plant.name: Plant Vogtle (Units 3 & 4)
signature_plant.fact: The first reactors built from scratch in the U.S. in more than 30 years — and, at about $35 billion, the most expensive power project in American history.
